questions.solution_html:
• Indirect Headlines in Advertising-Subtle and creative, often using wordplay, metaphors, or

questions.question: Briefly explain the digital transformation of advertising. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Interactivity (1994): The first banner ad (A T&T) shifted advertising from static images
  • to clickable, interactive content. Democratisation (2000): Google AdWords introduced
  • the pay-per-click model, making advertising affordable and measurable for businesses
  • of all sizes. Personalisation: Amazon and social media pioneered targeting based on
  • individual browsing history and specific user behaviours. Smart Integration: Modern
  • advertising uses AI and smartphone location data for hyper-personalised, real-time
  • communication. [U]/[CO1]

questions.question: Explain the concept of “genericisation” with examples from the advertising world. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Genericisation is the process by which a brand name becomes so dominant and synonymous
  • with a product or service that it is used as a common, generic term. It occurs through
  • consistently reinforcing a product’s unique strengths and market-leading qualities, which
  • creates the perception of absolute expertise in the consumer's mind. Eg. Google’s focus on
  • speed and reliability made it the leader in search. As a result, the phrase “Google it” has become
  • a generic verb for searching online, regardless of the search engine used.
  • [U] / [CO1]

questions.question: Compare and contrast trust words and scarcity words in terms of their psychological impact on consumers / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Trust Words (Psychological Security ): Words like "Guaranteed" or "Authentic" build
  • brand authority and reduce purchase anxiety. Their impact is to create long-term
  • confidence and reliability, which is essential for high-value decisions like financial
  • investments. Scarcity Words (Psychological Urgency): Terms like "Limited" or "Last
  • chance" trigger the "fear of missing out" (FOMO). Instead of security, they create
  • immediate pressure to bypass logical hesitation, as seen in Amazon’s “Only 2 left”
  • alerts. [U] / [CO2]

questions.question: Consider a food product advertisement that claims "clinically proven to boost immunity". How would you evaluate this claim using the advertising standards of ASCI, described in the text? / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Advertising Standards Council of India (ASCI)
  • Truthfulness and Accuracy: claim must be truthful, not misleading - based on scientific
  • evidence. Evaluation: advertiser must provide robust clinical data proving that the product
  • actually boosts immunity as stated - data should come from well-designed, peer-reviewed
  • studies conducted by credible institutions.
  • Health and safety: Health claims should be supported by reliable scientific data. Evaluation:
  • The study supporting the immunity-boosting claim must be independently verified and
  • published in a reputable journal, not just based on internal or unpublished research peer-
  • reviewed if presented as a medical or scientific fact.
  • Terms like "clinically proven" must not be used lightly or without substantial scientific
  • evidence-Evaluation: If the claim exaggerates the product’s effects without clear evidence, it
  • can be considered misleading. The term "clinically proven" should reflect rigorous scientific
  • testing, not just preliminary findings.
  • For this immunity-boosting claim to be ASCI-compliant, it must be backed by substantial,
  • peer-reviewed clinical evidence, avoid exaggeration, and provide a clear basis for the
  • "clinically proven" statement. If the ad lacks this level of support, it would likely be flagged
  • for misleading consumers. [CO2]

questions.question: How does the inverted pyramid format improve press releases? / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• It ensures the most critical journalistic information (Who, What, When, Where, Why,
  • and How) is presented at the very beginning to capture attention immediately. It
  • logically organizes the narrative by placing crucial evidence, quotes, and background
  • details in "The Body" only after the main hook is established. It leaves extra, related
  • context for "The Tail," allowing reporters to instantly grasp the core story while still
  • having access to additional details if needed. [U] / [CO3]

questions.question: Explain how direct, indirect and news headlines function, using examples to demonstrate their effectiveness. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Direct Headlines function by delivering straightforward, unambiguous statements that
  • immediately communicate a key benefit or offer. They avoid wordplay and are highly
  • effective for driving immediate action during sales or promotions. They typically
  • include specific numbers, prices, or clear promises. Eg : “50% Off on All Laptops for
  • Students”. Indirect Headlines function by using intrigue to create a "knowledge gap"
  • that draws the reader in. They are effective at engaging readers intellectually or
  • emotionally using clever wordplay, questions, or provocative statements that pique
  • curiosity without giving away the full message. They are particularly effective when
  • you want to engage readers emotionally or intellectually. Eg : “Your Morning Routine
  • is About to Change Forever”. [U] / [CO1]

questions.question: Describe in detail the various types of stereotyping in advertising. Provide examples of each type. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• i. Gender Stereotyping – Advertisements often portray women as homemakers,
  • caregivers and self-sacrificing mothers, while men are shown as dominant, career-
  • oriented and emotionally distant. Such portrayals reinforce traditional gender roles and
  • unrealistic expectations. Eg: Detergent ads showing women doing household chores;
  • male grooming ads linking masculinity with success and dominance. ii. Cultural and
  • Ethnic Stereotyping– Advertisements reduce minority communities and ethnic groups
  • to simplified clichés, stereotypical professions, accents or behaviours, often reinforcing
  • prejudice and social bias. Eg: Nivea’s “Re-Civilize Yourself” campaign and Intel’s
  • “Maximize Computing Performance” ad were criticized for racial insensitivity. iii. Age
  • Stereotyping – Advertisements create a generation gap by portraying older adults as
  • dependent, technologically confused, and resistant to change, while younger people are
  • shown as impulsive, superficial, and overly obsessed with social media. Eg: Digital
  • payment ads depicting seniors confused by apps like PhonePe or Google Pay . iv. Body
  • Image Stereotyping – Advertising promotes narrow standards of beauty by associating
  • attractiveness, confidence, and success with thinness, muscularity, or fair skin. Such
  • portrayals negatively affect self-esteem and body image. Eg: Fair & Lovely
  • advertisements promoting fair skin as the key to success; fitness ads equating
  • muscularity with masculinity. [K] / [CO2]

questions.question: Trace the evolution of PR showing how it shaped public perception and consumer behaviour. How far did the PR practices in America influence the growth of PR across the globe? / [CO3] [15x1 = 15]
questions.solution_html:
• Public Relations (PR) evolved from ancient rulers in Egypt, Babylon, and Greece using
  • communication to influence public opinion, to organised persuasion during the
  • American Revolution through slogans like “No Taxation without Representation.” The
  • Industrial Revolution and the growth of newspapers and mass media made public
  • opinion important for businesses and governments. Ivy Lee developed modern PR
  • through honest communication and crisis management, while Edward Bernays used
  • psychology and mass media to shape consumer behaviour and public opinion. In the
  • 20th century, PR expanded into government campaigns, corporate communication and
  • later digital media, social media, and reputation management. American PR practices
  • strongly influenced global PR by introducing professional communication methods,
  • crisis management, image building, and scientific audience persuasion techniques used
  • worldwide today. [U] / [CO3]
